title: composition and occasion
short: Written near Florence in autumn 1819, the ode was published in the Prometheus Unbound volume (1820); Shelley's note describes the storm that prompted it.
body: Shelley's own note says the poem was 'conceived and chiefly written in a wood that skirts the Arno, near Florence', on a day of the warm, rain-bringing wind, and that a violent storm of hail, thunder and lightning followed at sunset. The year 1819 was one of personal and political crisis: his son William died in June, and the Peterloo Massacre in Manchester (August) prompted The Mask of Anarchy and 'England in 1819'. Readers since have balanced a political reading (the wind as revolutionary force spreading the poet's ideas) with a personal one (the poet's depression and hope of renewal). The apostrophe 'O wild West Wind' sets the tone of urgent invocation.

title: terza rima and the stanza
short: Each of the five sections is fourteen lines: four terza-rima tercets (aba bcb cdc ded) closed by a couplet, a hybrid of Dante's measure and the sonnet.
body: Terza rima, the interlocking form of Dante's Divine Comedy, is fitting for a poem about forward motion: each tercet's middle rhyme drives the next. Closing every section with a couplet gives each a sonnet-like shape. Note that the archive text prints only sections I and V of the five; the omitted sections II-IV address the wind's action on clouds and on the sea before the poet turns, in IV, to his own weakness. Harold Bloom described the poem as a fusion of the public Pindaric ode with the personal Horatian ode.

title: breath
greek: Latin spiritus, Greek pneuma, Hebrew ruach: breath/wind/spirit
short: The wind is the "breath" or spirit of autumn: Latin spiritus and Greek pneuma mean both "wind" and "spirit".
body: The word-play on breath, wind and spirit runs through the ode: 'Wild Spirit' (l. 13), 'Be thou, Spirit fierce, / My spirit!' (ll. 61-62). The same identity is ancient: in Genesis 1:2 the 'Spirit of God' moving on the waters translates the Hebrew ruach, which also means wind, and in John 3:8 'the wind bloweth where it listeth'. Shelley, a declared atheist, takes over the language of inspiration (literally, 'breathing in') and redirects it to a natural force.

anchor: like ghosts from an enchanter fleeing
title: leaves like ghosts
short: The simile of dead leaves as fleeing souls draws on an epic tradition from Homer and Virgil through Dante and Milton.
body: Comparing the dead to falling leaves is one of the oldest epic similes (Iliad 6; Aeneid 6.309-10). Dante uses it of the damned souls crowding Charon's boat (Inferno 3.112-117), and Milton of the fallen angels lying 'Thick as autumnal leaves that strow the brooks / In Vallombrosa' (Paradise Lost 1.302-3); Vallombrosa is in the hills near Florence, where Shelley was writing. The 'enchanter' adds a touch of romance magic: the wind is a sorcerer driving spirits before it.

title: hectic
short: The feverish flush of consumption (tuberculosis), the "hectic fever"; the leaves' colours are those of disease.
body: 'Hectic' (from Greek hektikos, 'habitual, consumptive') was the medical term for the recurring fever of wasting diseases, and 'hectic red' was the flush on a consumptive's cheek. The four colours (yellow, black, pale, red) have sometimes been read as the colours of the human races, or as the stages of a disease. Either way, the dead leaves become a sick crowd, which leads into 'Pestilence-stricken multitudes'. Keats, a consumptive, was dying as this poem was published, and Shelley would mourn him in Adonais (1821).

title: Pestilence-stricken multitudes
short: The leaves become plague-struck crowds, an image with a political edge in the year of Peterloo.
body: The phrase completes the turn from nature to humanity begun by 'ghosts'. 'Multitudes' was a loaded word in post-war England, when mass meetings for reform were being dispersed by force; in The Mask of Anarchy (1819) Shelley addresses the people as 'Ye are many'. The wind sweeps away the sick and dead to make room for new life: the political reading sees here a cleansing revolutionary force.

title: chariotest
short: An invented verb: you carry (the seeds) as in a chariot.
body: Shelley makes a verb from the noun 'chariot', with the archaic second-person ending -est. The chariot suggests a classical god of the winds, or a triumphal procession, and contrasts with the 'dark wintry bed' to which the seeds are carried. The seeds are buried 'each like a corpse within its grave', but the burial is a planting: the image of the seed that dies and is raised anticipates the hope of the close.

anchor: like a corpse within its grave
title: the buried seed
short: The seed buried as a corpse awaiting resurrection echoes St Paul and the Gospel of John on the grain that must die to bear fruit.
body: St Paul writes that what is sown 'is not quickened, except it die' (1 Corinthians 15:36), and Christ says that unless a grain of wheat dies it 'abideth alone' (John 12:24). Shelley borrows this resurrection logic for a natural cycle, without the Christian promise. The word 'quicken' returns in section V ('to quicken a new birth'), so the image frames the whole ode.

sources.cite: Bible (KJV), 1 Corinthians 15:36; John 12:24

anchor: Thine azure sister of the Spring
title: azure sister of the Spring
short: The gentle west wind of spring (the classical Zephyrus), "sister" to the wild autumn wind.
body: In classical poetry the west wind (Greek Zephyros, Latin Favonius) is the warm wind of spring. Shelley makes the autumn and spring winds siblings: the same west wind both destroys and revives. 'Azure', sky-blue, contrasts with the dark and sickly colours of the leaves. Her trumpet-call ('clarion') wakes the earth from its dream of winter. The feminine pronoun also sets up a family of natural powers, in keeping with the poem's animism.

title: clarion
short: A shrill trumpet; the spring wind sounds a call that wakes the "dreaming earth", echoing the trumpet of the resurrection.
body: The clarion recalls the last trumpet of 1 Corinthians 15:52, at whose sound 'the dead shall be raised'. Shelley's resurrection is seasonal, not eschatological. The image prepares the 'trumpet of a prophecy' at the poem's end, so that the first and last sections are linked by trumpet calls: the spring wind's in nature, the poet's in human affairs. The word also had military associations (a clarion called troops to battle).

anchor: Wild Spirit, which art moving everywhere
title: Wild Spirit
short: The wind as an all-pervading spirit, in language close to that of prayer to God.
body: 'Which art' echoes the Lord's Prayer ('Our Father which art in heaven', Matthew 6:9), and the phrase recalls the spirit 'moving' on the waters of Genesis 1:2. The ode takes the form of a prayer throughout: invocation, a list of the deity's powers, and the refrain 'hear, oh hear!'. Shelley turns the liturgical form toward nature, and later toward himself.

sources.cite: Bible (KJV), Matthew 6:9; Genesis 1:2

title: Destroyer and preserver
short: The wind's double action: it kills the leaves and saves the seeds; destruction and renewal are one process.
body: This paradox is the poem's central idea. The wind strips the trees and scatters the seeds that will grow again. Some readers compare the pairing with the Hindu gods Shiva (destroyer) and Vishnu (preserver), with whom Shelley may have been familiar through the Orientalist writing of his time; this is a comparison rather than a demonstrated source. Politically, the phrase implies that revolution must destroy before it renews. The refrain 'hear, oh hear!' ends sections I to III.

title: Make me thy lyre
short: The poet asks to become an Aeolian harp, the stringed instrument sounded by the wind, a key Romantic image of inspiration.
body: The Aeolian (wind) harp was placed in an open window so that the breeze made it sound; Coleridge's 'The Eolian Harp' (1795) made it an emblem of the mind. Shelley's Defence of Poetry compares man to 'an instrument' over which impressions pass 'like the alternations of an ever-changing wind over an Aeolian lyre'. Here the poet wants to be played as the forest is played, but the Defence adds that the mind also responds actively; the ode moves from passive instrument to active prophet.

anchor: What if my leaves are falling
title: my leaves are falling
short: The poet identifies himself with the autumn forest: his "leaves" are both his declining years and the pages of his writing.
body: The pun on leaves as pages runs through the final section: the 'dead thoughts' are driven 'like withered leaves' over the universe. Shelley was only twenty-seven, but section IV speaks of a life that has fallen 'upon the thorns of life' and is 'chained and bowed'. His work had a small readership, and the hope here is that even dead pages can be scattered and fertilise a new age. The 'deep, autumnal tone' acknowledges a mature, sadder music.

title: Be thou me
short: The climax of the poet's identification with the wind; the grammar is startling ("be thou me", not "be thou in me").
body: The repetition 'Be thou, Spirit fierce, / My spirit! Be thou me' moves from possession to identity. Some critics read it as the high point of Romantic self-assertion, others as self-annihilation, the poet surrendering his personality to a natural force. The odd pronoun 'me' (where grammar might expect 'I') makes the merging physical. 'Impetuous', rushing forward (Latin impetus, 'attack'), is the wind's defining quality.

title: quicken
short: To give life to (as in "the quick and the dead"); the withered leaves are to fertilise a new age.
body: 'Quicken' meant to make alive, and also referred to the first movement of a child in the womb, so 'quicken a new birth' joins agriculture and pregnancy. The word recalls St Paul's 'that which thou sowest is not quickened, except it die' (1 Corinthians 15:36), linking back to the seeds of section I. The leaves rot and become the soil of new life: Shelley's hope that his work, ignored now, will feed later readers and reforms.

anchor: by the incantation of this verse
title: incantation
short: A spell chanted aloud (Latin incantare, "to sing over"); the poem becomes a magic formula that compels the wind.
body: With this word the ode becomes self-conscious: its verse is the instrument by which the poet hopes to command the wind. This recalls the 'enchanter' of l. 3 (the same Latin root, cantare, 'to sing'), so that the poet now takes the enchanter's place. The ode thus claims for poetry the power of a spell, a claim Shelley makes more broadly in A Defence of Poetry.

title: unextinguished hearth
short: The poet's mind is a fire not yet out; its ashes and sparks, scattered by the wind, may kindle new fires.
body: The image combines dead matter (ashes) and living fire (sparks), echoing the destroyer and preserver of section I. A spark carried by the wind can start a blaze: the metaphor of ideas as sparks had strong revolutionary associations in the period. 'Unextinguished' insists that the poet's inspiration, though dimmed, is still alive. Shelley's Defence calls the mind in creation 'a fading coal' which some invisible influence, 'like an inconstant wind', awakens to brightness.

title: trumpet of a prophecy
short: The poet as prophet; the image recalls the trumpets of the Old Testament prophets and of the Apocalypse.
body: Biblical prophets are told to lift up their voices 'like a trumpet' (Isaiah 58:1), and trumpets announce the end in Revelation. Shelley's prophecy is secular: the coming of a better political and moral order. The phrase answers the spring wind's 'clarion' in section I, so the poet takes on the wind's role. The line runs over into 'O Wind', breaking the sentence and the couplet pattern in a burst of urgency.

title: If Winter comes ...
short: The rhetorical question expects the answer "no"; but as a question it leaves room for doubt.
body: The final line is among the most quoted in English. Read confidently, it states the law of the seasons as a law of history: oppression and despair must give way to renewal. Read closely, it is a question, not a statement, and follows a poem of desperate prayer; several critics stress the uncertainty, the hope that has to be asked for. The seasonal cycle had already been made political in the reform movement: Shelley's question invites the reader to supply the answer.
